title: Reading practice: The Canal and the Bridge Debate
description: A history of the Erie Canal and a town council debate: sequence, cause and effect, vocabulary in context, and comparing arguments.

stimuli.title: Building the Erie Canal
paragraphs: More than two hundred years ago, many farmers in New York lived far from the coast. They grew crops to sell, but they had no easy way to send them to the cities on the coast. There were no trains yet, and the roads were rough. A wagon trip could take weeks, and sending goods cost a great deal of money.

People in New York decided to build a canal. A canal is a waterway made by people. In 1817, workers began to dig the Erie Canal. They used shovels and picks, and animals helped pull away the dirt. The finished canal ran about 363 miles, from the Hudson River near Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo.

The land was not flat, so the builders also made locks. A lock is a part of the canal with gates at both ends. A boat enters the lock, the gates close, and water is let in or out to lift or lower the boat. In this way, boats could travel up and down hills.

The canal opened in 1825. Mules walked on a path beside the water, called a towpath, and pulled the boats. Now a farmer could send grain to New York City in days instead of weeks, and for less money. As a result, more goods moved, more people traveled west, and towns along the canal, such as Rochester and Buffalo, grew into busy cities.

stimuli.title: Town Council Meeting: A Bridge or a Ferry?
paragraphs: The town of Riverside sits beside a wide river. A small ferry carries people and cars across, but it stops running at 6:00 in the evening. The town council must decide whether to build a bridge. Two council members speak at the meeting.

Ms. Ortiz says, “We should build the bridge. The ferry can carry only ten cars at one time, so long lines form every morning. Farmers wait for hours to bring food to the market. A bridge would let people cross at any time of day, and fire trucks could reach the other side quickly. For these reasons, a bridge is the best choice for our town.”

Mr. Lund says, “We should keep the ferry. I agree that the lines are long, but a bridge would cost a great deal of money, and our town has a small budget. Many families depend on the jobs of the ferry workers. We could buy a second ferry for much less than a bridge costs. Then the lines would be shorter, and no ferry worker would lose a job. A second ferry is the best choice for our town.”

items.stem: Put the events from the history in the order they happened.

items.text: Towns along the canal grew into busy cities.
Farmers had trouble sending their crops to the coast.
Workers began to dig the canal in 1817.

items.explanation: The farmers’ problem came first. Workers began digging in 1817, the canal opened in 1825, and then towns grew.

support.clue: Look at the dates 1817 and 1825, and at the words “As a result.” Ask what problem started the story and what came last.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different history). A village had no bridge, so people crossed a stream on stepping stones. Then neighbors built a wooden footbridge. Later, the village added a stone bridge. At last, a market grew near the stone bridge. The order shows a problem, an action, and a result.

Now put the canal events in order in the same way.

facts: Construction of the Erie Canal began in 1817.
Towns such as Rochester and Buffalo grew along the canal.

items.stem: Match each cause from the history with its effect.

left.text: The roads were rough, and there were no trains.
The canal made shipping faster and cheaper.

right.text: Towns along the canal grew into busy cities.
Sending goods to the coast was slow and costly.
Builders made locks to lift and lower boats.

items.explanation: Rough roads and no trains made shipping slow and costly. Land that was not flat led to locks. Faster, cheaper shipping helped towns grow.

support.clue: Find the connecting words “so” and “As a result,” and look for what comes before them.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different history). Long ago, a town had a river that flooded each spring. Because the river flooded, people built houses on a hill. Because the hill was far from the river, people carried water in buckets. A cause leads to an effect, and an effect can become the next cause.

Now match each cause in the canal history with its effect.

facts: The Erie Canal used locks to lift and lower boats.
Towns such as Rochester and Buffalo grew along the canal.

items.stem: Choose the best words to explain why the canal was built and what changed.

dropdown.template: {1} the roads were rough, farmers could not sell their grain far away. {2}, people decided to build a canal. After the canal opened, a farmer could send grain to New York City in {3} instead of weeks.

items.explanation: Rough roads were the cause. The canal was the result. The text says grain could then travel in days instead of weeks.

support.clue: Read the first paragraph for the problem and the last paragraph for the change. Look at the words “instead of weeks.”
support.frame: The first connecting word shows a ______, and the second connecting word shows a ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different cause and effect). “Since the path was icy, the class walked slowly. For that reason, they arrived late.” The first connecting word gives the reason, and the second one gives what followed.

Now use two connecting words like these to explain why the canal was built.

facts: A wagon trip across New York in the early 1800s was slow and costly.
The Erie Canal cut travel time and shipping costs.

items.stem: In this history, what is a lock?

options.text: A metal key or latch that workers use to keep the canal gates shut at night.
A path beside the canal where mules walked while they pulled the boats along.
A part of the canal with gates, where water is let in or out to move a boat up or down.
A tool that workers used with shovels and picks when they dug the canal.

distractors.a: This uses another meaning of the word. In the text, a lock is part of the canal, not a key.
distractors.b: The path beside the water is called a towpath.
distractors.d: Workers dug with shovels and picks. A lock is part of the finished canal.

items.explanation: The text defines a lock as a part of the canal with gates, where water is let in or out to lift or lower a boat.

support.clue: Find the sentence that starts “A lock is.” Use the sentences after it to see what happens inside a lock.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different word). In a text about farms, “a silo is a tall building where farmers store grain.” The text gives a category (a tall building) and a job (store grain). Look for the same two pieces of information.

Now find the category and the job for the word lock.

misconceptions.a: uses the everyday meaning of the word
misconceptions.d: confuses a canal part with a tool

facts: A canal lock is a chamber with gates where water is raised or lowered to move a boat to a different level.

items.stem: Match each speaker, or both speakers, with the idea in the speeches.

right.text: A second ferry would cost much less than a bridge.
The town should do nothing and keep the ferry just as it is.
Long lines form at the ferry, and that is a problem.
A bridge would let people cross at any time of day.

items.explanation: Ms. Ortiz says a bridge lets people cross at any hour. Mr. Lund says a second ferry costs less. Both speakers say that long lines form at the ferry.

support.clue: Read each speech. Ask which idea appears in only one speech and which idea appears in both.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different debate). One student wants a longer recess because kids need time to play. Another student wants an extra art class because kids need time to create. Both students want kids to have a better school day. An idea can be different for each speaker and still be shared.

Now match each idea in the bridge debate with the right speaker or with both.

items.stem: Sort each reason: does it support building a bridge or keeping the ferry?

tokens.text: The ferry carries only ten cars at one time.
A bridge would cost a great deal of money.
Fire trucks could reach the other side quickly.
Many families depend on the ferry workers’ jobs.

items.explanation: Ms. Ortiz uses the ten-car limit and fire trucks to support a bridge. Mr. Lund uses the cost and the ferry jobs to support keeping the ferry.

support.clue: Find the speaker who says each sentence. Check which last sentence names that speaker’s choice.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different debate). Should the class pet be a fish or a hamster? Reason for the fish: it is quiet and easy to feed. Reason for the hamster: it can be held and played with. Each reason belongs to the side it helps.

Now sort the reasons for the bridge and the ferry in the same way.

items.stem: Choose the best words to finish the description of what Ms. Ortiz says and how she argues.

dropdown.template: Ms. Ortiz states her claim: the town should {1}. Her first reason is that the ferry {2}, so long lines form. At the end, she {3} her claim.

options: carries only ten cars at one time
costs the town too much money
needs two more workers to run
2.answer: carries only ten cars at one time

items.explanation: Ms. Ortiz says the town should build a bridge. Her first reason is that the ferry carries only ten cars at one time, so long lines form. In her last sentence she says again that a bridge is the best choice.

support.clue: Read Ms. Ortiz’s speech, not Mr. Lund’s. Compare her first sentence with her last sentence, and find the reason that comes right after “so long lines form.”
support.frame: Ms. Ortiz wants the town to ______ because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different speech). A student asks for a class pet. She begins with what she wants, then tells two good things about a fish: it is quiet and easy to feed. She ends by saying what she wants one more time. Each part of a speech has its own job.

Now describe what Ms. Ortiz says and how she says it.

items.stem: According to Mr. Lund, what would happen if the town bought a second ferry? Choose two.

options.text: The town would spend a great deal of money on a ferry.
The lines to cross the river would be shorter.
People could cross the river at any time of day.
No ferry worker would lose his or her job.

distractors.a: Mr. Lund says a second ferry costs much less than a bridge. The great cost belongs to the bridge.
distractors.c: Crossing at any time of day is Ms. Ortiz’s reason for a bridge. The ferry stops running at 6:00 in the evening.

items.explanation: Mr. Lund says that with a second ferry the lines would be shorter and no ferry worker would lose a job.

support.clue: Reread Mr. Lund’s speech from the sentence that starts “We could buy a second ferry.” Find the effects that come after the word “Then.”
support.frame: If the town buys a second ferry, then ______ and ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different plan). A coach says, “If we add a second practice, then the team will play better and more students will join.” The words after “if” name the plan. The words after “then” name the results.

Now find the two results that follow Mr. Lund’s plan.

misconceptions.c: gives a speaker’s reason to the other speaker
